label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
 Let $0 < \varepsilon < 2/5$ and let $D$ be the Dirac operator of the $4$-cycle $1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 1$ with entries
 \[ d_{12} = \varepsilon, d_{23} = d_{34} = d_{41} = 1.\]
 Then,
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant \kappa(\varepsilon) \colonequals \frac{2}{\sqrt{5\varepsilon^2 - 2\varepsilon + 1}},\]
 while deleting the edge $\{1,2\}$ yields $d^{D'}(1,2) = 2 < d^{D}(1,2)$.  In particular, if $\varepsilon = 1/5$, then $d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant \sqrt{5} > 2$.
head: environment

label: thm:sharp
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sharp}
 Over all weighted $4$-cycles,
 \[ \dfrac{d^{D}(1,2)}{d^{D'}(1,2)} \leqslant \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\]
and this upper bound is attained when $w_{12} = 3$, $w_{14} = w_{23} = 1/\sqrt{2}$, and $w_{34} = 1$, in which case $d^{D}(1,2) = \sqrt{3}$ and $d^{D'}(1,2) = 3/2$.
head: environment

label: thm:supbound
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:supbound}
 Let $D$ be a Dirac operator on a finite graph, let $e$ be any edge, and let $D'$ be obtained from $D$ by deleting $e$.  Then, for all vertices $x$ and $y$,
 \[ d^{D}(x,y) \leqslant \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}d^{D'}(x,y).\]
 Moreover, the constant $2/\sqrt{3}$ is sharp and is obtained by the weighted $4$-cycle of Theorem \ref{thm:sharp}, where $x$ and $y$ are the endpoints of the deleted edge.
head: environment

label: thm:cycles
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cycles}
 Let $n \geqslant 3$ and let $D$ be a Dirac operator on the $n$-cycle.  For an edge $e$, define $D'$ to be the Dirac operator obtained by deleting the edge $e$.  If $4 \nmid n$, then
 \[ d^{D'}(x,y) \geqslant d^{D}(x,y)\]
 for all edges $e$ and for all choices $x,y$ of vertices.  On the other hand, if $4 \mid n$, then there exists a Dirac operator $D$, an edge $e$, and vertices $x, y$ such that
 \[ d^{D'}(x,y) < d^{D}(x,y).\]

For all vertices $x,y$, $d^{D}(x,y) \leqslant \ell^D(x,y)$, and $d^{D}(x,y) = \ell^D(x,y)$ when $\{x,y\}$ is a bridge.

label: prop:deletion
title: Proposition
body_md:

If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by setting to $0$ the $i^{\text{th}}$ row and column (which corresponds to the deletion of the vertex $i$), then $d^{D'} \geqslant d^{D}$.  More generally, if $V'$ is a subset of vertices of $V$ and $d^{D}_{V'}$ is the associated noncommutative distance on the induced subgraph, then $d^{D}_{V'} \geqslant d^{D}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $0 < \varepsilon < 2/5$, let $\kappa = \kappa(\varepsilon)$, and let
 \[ A = \operatorname{diag}\left( \kappa, 0, \kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2}, \kappa\frac{1 + \varepsilon}{2}\right).\]
 If $M = (m_{ij}) = [A,D]$, then $m_{ij} = (a_i - a_j)d_{ij}$, $M$ is skew-symmetric, and
 \[ M = \begin{pmatrix}
         0          & \kappa\varepsilon & 0      & \kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2}\\
         -\kappa\varepsilon & 0         & -\kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2} & 0\\
         0          & \kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2} & 0 & -\kappa\varepsilon\\
         -\kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2} & 0 & \kappa\varepsilon & 0\\
        \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Moreover,
\[MM^t = \left((\kappa\varepsilon)^2 + \left(\kappa\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2} \right)^2\right)I = I,\]
so $\left\lVert [A,D] \right\rVert = \left\lVert M \right\rVert = 1$, $A$ is admissible in \eqref{eq:def}, and $d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant a_1 - a_2 = \kappa$.

On the other hand, deleting the edge $\{1,2\}$ leaves a path on four vertices with endpoints $1$, $2$ and all edges having weight $1$.  By Propositions \ref{prop:prune} and \ref{prop:chain}, $d^{D'}(1,2) = 2$.

Since $0 < \varepsilon < 2/5$, $\varepsilon(5\varepsilon - 2) < 0$, and so $\kappa = \kappa(\varepsilon) > 2$, completing the proof that $d^{D}(1,2) > d^{D'}(1,2)$.  Finally, since $5\varepsilon^2 - 2\varepsilon + 1$ is minimized at $\varepsilon = 1/5$, the largest value of $\kappa$ is $\sqrt{5}$.

label: rem:ikm
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:ikm}
 \begin{itemize}
  \item[(1)] Setting $d_1 = w_{12}$, $d_2 = w_{13} = \infty$, $d_3 = w_{14}$, $d_4 = w_{23}$, $d_5 = w_{24} = \infty$, and $d_6 = w_{34}$ recovers the notation of \cite[Theorem 9]{IKM01}.
  \item[(2)] The hypothesis is stated there as ``$1/d_2 = 1/d_5 = \infty$'' and in the proof as ``$d_2 = d_5 = 0$''; the hypothesis actually used is ``$d_2 = d_5 = \infty$''.
  \item[(3)] There is a simplification to the third branch of $d^{D}(1,2)$ from the printed version.  Let
  \[ x_2 = \frac{w_{12}(w_{14} + w_{23})}{\sqrt{(w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2}}, \qquad x_3 = \frac{w_{12}|w_{14} - w_{23}|}{\sqrt{(w_{14} - w_{23})^2} + (w_{12} + w_{34})^2};\]
  in the original statement, the third branch was $\max(x_2, x_3)$, and it turns out $x_2 \geqslant x_3$ always.  When comparing $x_2$ to $x_3$, we can cancel the common factor $w_{12}$, and after some simplifying,
  we find that
  \[ x_2 \geqslant x_3 \iff \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{w_{12} - w_{34}}{w_{14} + w_{23}}\right)^2}} \geqslant \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{w_{12} + w_{34}}{w_{14} - w_{23}} \right)^2}}.\]
  Noting that the function $t \mapsto 1/\sqrt{1 + (c/t)^2}$ is strictly decreasing as a function of $c/t$, this implies that
  \[ x_2 \geqslant x_3 \iff \frac{|w_{12} - w_{34}|}{w_{14} + w_{23}} \leqslant \frac{w_{12} + w_{34}}{|w_{14} - w_{23}|}.\]
  This further implies
  \[ x_2 \geqslant x_3 \iff (w_{14} + w_{23})(w_{12} + w_{34}) \geqslant |w_{14} - w_{23}| \cdot |w_{12} - w_{34}|.\]
  This last inequality is immediate from the triangle inequality since all $w_{ij}$ are nonnegative.  Hence $x_2 \geqslant x_3$.
  \item[(4)] The separate ``$d_1d_6 = d_3d_4$'' branch from $d^{D}(1,2)$ can be dropped: in that case, the first factor of $C$ equals $(d_3 + d_4)^2d_6 + d_6(d_1 - d_6)^2 > 0$ and the second is also positive, so $C > 0$ and the third branch applies (and, in fact, the formula from the ``$d_1d_6 = d_3d_4$'' branch coincides with our formula above when $C > 0$, subject to the assumption that $d_1d_6 = d_3d_4$).
  \item[(5)] The numerator in the third branch of $d^{D}(1,2)$ was printed in the statement as $d_1\sqrt{d_3^2 + d_4^2}$; however, the correct value printed above is what was used in the proof.
  \item[(6)] The left sides of the inequalities in the first two branches of $d^{D}(1,3)$ need to be squared; again, this is what was used in the original proof.
  \item[(7)] The result printed above was verified numerically using a semidefinite-program computation by Claude Opus 5 over 1000 random weighted $4$-cycles, which included at least 100 examples corresponding to each branch in each formula.
 \end{itemize}

label: lem:notbranch1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:notbranch1}
 Using the notation above, if $d^{D}(1,2) > d^{D'}(1,2)$, then $w_{12} > w_{34}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $w_{12} \leqslant w_{34}$.  By Proposition \ref{prop:ikm}, $d^{D}(1,2) = w_{12} \leqslant w_{34}$.  Based on the formula for $d^{D'}(1,2) = \lambda$, we divide into cases based on whether $w_{34}$ is greater than or less than or equal to $\sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$.  If $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, then
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}} \leqslant \frac{w_{14} + w_{23}}{2} < \sigma = \lambda. \]
 On the other hand, if $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, then $\sqrt{w_{14}^2 + w_{34}^2} \sqrt{w_{23}^2 + w_{34}^2} \geqslant w_{34}^2$ implies
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant w_{34} \leqslant \Lambda = \lambda.\]  The result follows.
head: environment

label: lem:C
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:C}
 Assume $w_{12} > w_{34}$.  Using the notation above, $C \leqslant 0$ if and only if $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$ and
 \[ w_{12} \geqslant w_{34} + \frac{\sigma^2 w_{34}}{w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23}}.\]
 Moreover, if $C \leqslant 0$, then $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$ and $w_{12}w_{34} > w_{14}w_{23}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $(w_{14} - w_{23})^2w_{34} +(w_{12} + w_{34})(w_{14}w_{23} + w_{34}^2)$ is always positive for positive $w_{ij}$, we have that $C \leqslant 0$ if and only if $(w_{14} + w_{23})^2w_{34} +(w_{12} - w_{34})(w_{14}w_{23} - w_{34}^2) \leqslant 0.$  If $w_{34}^2 \leqslant w_{14}w_{23}$, then the first factor of $C$ is the sum of a nonnegative term and a positive term, and hence $C > 0$.  When $w_{34}^2 > w_{14}w_{23}$, we rearrange the first inequality; this proves the first claim.

 Next, since $w_{12} > w_{34}$, $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$ implies $C > 0$, so, if $C \leqslant 0$, then $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$.  Finally, if $C \leqslant 0$ and $w_{12} > w_{34}$, we have
 \[ w_{14}w_{23} < w_{34}^2 < w_{12}w_{34}.\]
head: environment

label: thm:alwaysaw12
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:alwaysaw12}
 Using the notation above, for any choice of $w_{14}, w_{23}, w_{34}$, $d^{D}(1,2) > d^{D'}(1,2)$ for all $w_{12}$ sufficiently large.  In particular, if $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, then $d^{D}(1,2) > d^{D'}(1,2)$ whenever $w_{12} \geqslant w_{34} + \sigma^2 w_{34}/(w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23})$, and if $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, then $d^{D}(1,2) > d^{D'}(1,2)$ whenever $w_{12} > (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/(2w_{34}).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first $w_{34} > \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$ and $w_{12} \geqslant w_{34} + \sigma^2 w_{34}/(w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23})$.  This implies $d^{D'}(1,2) = \lambda = \Lambda$ and so
 \begin{align*}
  d^{D}(1,2) &= \dfrac{w_{12}\sqrt{w_{14}^2 + w_{34}^2}\sqrt{w_{23}^2 + w_{34}^2}}{|w_{14}w_{23} - w_{12}w_{34}|} && \text{Proposition \ref{prop:ikm} and Lemma \ref{lem:C}}\\
           &= \dfrac{w_{12}w_{34}\Lambda}{|w_{14}w_{23} - w_{12}w_{34}|} && \\
           &= \dfrac{w_{12}w_{34}\Lambda}{w_{12}w_{34} - w_{14}w_{23}} && \text{Lemma \ref{lem:C}}\\
           &= \dfrac{\Lambda}{1 - \frac{w_{14}w_{23}}{w_{12}w_{34}}} && \\
           &> \Lambda && \text{Lemma \ref{lem:C}}\\
           &= d^{D'}(1,2).
 \end{align*}

Next, assume $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$ and $w_{12} > (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/(2w_{34}).$  Since $\sigma^2 \geqslant 4w_{14}w_{23} \geqslant 4w_{34}^2$, we have
\[w_{12} > \frac{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}{2w_{34}} \geqslant \frac{5w_{34}}{2} > w_{34}.\]  Further, since $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, we have $d^{D'}(1,2) = \lambda = \sigma$ and, by Lemma \ref{lem:C}, $C > 0$, so
\[ d^{D}(1,2) = \dfrac{w_{12}(w_{14} + w_{23})}{\sqrt{(w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2}}.\]  Since $w_{12} > (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/(2w_{34})$ and $\lambda = \sigma$, we have
\[ (\sigma^2 - \lambda^2)w_{12}^2 + 2\lambda^2w_{34}w_{12} - \lambda^2(\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2) = 2\lambda^2w_{34}w_{12} - \lambda^2(\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2) > 0,\]
which is equivalent to
\[ d^{D}(1,2) = \dfrac{w_{12}(w_{14} + w_{23})}{\sqrt{(w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2}} = \dfrac{w_{12}\sigma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2}} > \lambda = d^{D'}(1,2).\]
The result follows.

label: prop:dD12bound
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dD12bound}
 Using the notation above, for fixed $w_{14}, w_{23}, w_{34}$, $d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant \sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}$, and this upper bound is attained when $w_{12} = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/w_{34}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove first that each piecewise branch of the formula for $d^{D}(1,2)$ from Proposition \ref{prop:ikm} is bounded above by $\sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}$.

 Assume first that $w_{12} \leqslant w_{34}$.  Then,
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) = w_{12} \leqslant w_{34} < \sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}.\]

 Next, assume $w_{12} > w_{34}$ and $C \leqslant 0$.  As in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:alwaysaw12}, we see that
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) = \dfrac{\Lambda}{1 - \frac{w_{14}w_{23}}{w_{12}w_{34}}},\]
 and this function is decreasing in $w_{12}$, and, by Lemma \ref{lem:C}, the minimum value of $w_{12}$ is
 \[ w_{12} = w_{34} + \frac{\sigma^2 w_{34}}{w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23}}.\]
 Using this value for $w_{12}$ and noting that
 \[ \dfrac{w_{14}w_{23}(w_{14} + w_{23})^2(w_{14}^2 + w_{34}^2)(w_{23}^2 + w_{34}^2)}{(w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23})^2} > 0,\]
 after rearrangement we have
 \[ (2w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23})w_{12}^2 - 2w_{34}((w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + w_{34}^2)w_{12} + w_{14}w_{23}((w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + w_{34}^2) > 0.\]
 After multiplying through by $w_{14}w_{23}$ and rearranging, we have
 \[ d^{D}(1,2)^2 = \dfrac{w_{12}^2(w_{14}^2 + w_{34}^2)(w_{23}^2 + w_{34}^2)}{(w_{12}w_{34} - w_{14}w_{23})^2} < (w_{14} + w_{23})^2 + w_{34}^2 = \left(\sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}\right)^2,\] which shows $d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant \sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}$ for this branch as well.

 For the final branch, we assume $w_{12} > w_{34}$ and $C > 0$.  In this case, we note that
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eq:supd12}
  (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)(\sigma^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2) - w_{12}^2\sigma^2 = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2 - w_{12}w_{34})^2 \geqslant 0
 \end{equation}
 (with equality precisely when $w_{12} = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/w_{34}$), and this inequality rearranges to give us
 \[ d^{D}(1,2)^2 = \dfrac{w_{12}^2\sigma^2}{\sigma^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2} \leqslant \sigma^2 + w_{34}^2 = \left(\sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}\right)^2,\]
 which shows that $d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant \sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}$ in any case.

 Finally, assume $w_{12} = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/w_{34}$.  Note that $w_{12} = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/w_{34} > w_{34}$.  If $w_{34} \leqslant \sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}}$, then $C > 0$ by Lemma \ref{lem:C}.  Otherwise, $w_{34}^2 > w_{14}w_{23}$, and, since
 \[ \dfrac{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}{w_{34}} - w_{34} - \dfrac{\sigma^2w_{34}}{w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23}} = \dfrac{-w_{14}w_{23}\sigma^2}{w_{34}(w_{34}^2 - w_{14}w_{23})} < 0,\]
 by Lemma \ref{lem:C} we again have $C > 0$. In either case, by Proposition \ref{prop:ikm}
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) = \dfrac{w_{12}\sigma}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + (w_{12} - w_{34})^2}}.\]  By \eqref{eq:supd12} above, this shows $d^{D}(1,2) = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}$ when $w_{12} = (\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2)/w_{34}$, as desired.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We once more use the notation introduced above.  By Proposition \ref{prop:dD12bound},
 \[ \dfrac{d^{D}(1,2)}{d^{D'}(1,2)} \leqslant \dfrac{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}}{\lambda}.\]
 Since $\sqrt{\sigma^2 + w_{34}^2}/\lambda$ is invariant under simultaneous scaling of all edge weights, we set $w_{34} = 1$ and define $\rho:= w_{14}w_{23}$.  Note that by Lemma \ref{lem:notbranch1}, $w_{12} > 1$, and, by \eqref{eq:4path}, we have two cases: $\rho \geqslant 1$ and $\rho < 1$.  Set $R \colonequals \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 1}/\lambda$.

 Assume first that $\rho \geqslant 1$.  By \eqref{eq:4path}, $\lambda = \sigma$, and
 \[ R = \dfrac{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 1}}{\sigma} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{\sigma^2}}.\]
 Since $R$ is decreasing in $\sigma$ and
 \[\sigma = w_{14} + w_{23} \geqslant 2\sqrt{w_{14}w_{23}} = 2\sqrt{\rho} \geqslant 2,\]
 we have
 \[ R \leqslant \dfrac{2^2 + 1}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2} < \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\]

 Now assume $\rho < 1$.  By \eqref{eq:4path}, we have
 \[ \lambda = \Lambda = \sqrt{(w_{14}^2 + 1)(w_{23}^2 + 1)} = \sqrt{(1 - \rho)^2 + \sigma^2},\]
 and so $R = \dfrac{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + 1}}{\sqrt{(1 - \rho)^2 + \sigma^2}}$; note that for a fixed $\sigma$ that $R$ increases with $\rho$.  Since
 \[ \rho = w_{14}w_{23} \leqslant \dfrac{(w_{14} + w_{23})^2}{4} = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{4},\] we may set $\rho = \min(1, \sigma^2/4)$.  When $\sigma \geqslant 2$, as $\rho \to 1^-$ we have $R \to \sqrt{\sigma^2 + 1}/\sigma \leqslant \sqrt{5}/2 < 2/\sqrt{3}$ by the work above.  When $\sigma < 2$, we have $\rho = \sigma^2/4$, which occurs when $w_{14} = w_{23} = \sigma/2$.  Thus,
 \[ R^2 = \dfrac{\sigma^2 + 1}{(1 - \sigma^2/4)^2 + \sigma^2} = \dfrac{\sigma^2 + 1}{(1 + \sigma^2/4)^2}.\]
 As a function of $\sigma^2$, the maximum occurs when $\sigma^2 = 2$, and so $\sigma = \sqrt{2}$, $\rho = \sigma^2/4 = 1/2$, and $R = 2/\sqrt{3}$.  This corresponds to $w_{34} = 1$, $w_{14} = w_{23} = 1/\sqrt{2}$, and (by Proposition \ref{prop:dD12bound}) $w_{12} = 3$; indeed, $d^{D}(1,2) = \sqrt{3}$ and $d^{D'}(1,2) = 3/2$.

label: lem:ineq
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since both sides of the inequality are symmetric in $P, Q$, we may assume $P \leqslant Q$.  By the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality,
 \[ 2\sqrt{(\delta^2 + P^2)(\delta^2 + Q^2)} = 2\sqrt{3(\delta^2 + P^2) \cdot \frac{\delta^2 + Q^2}{3}} \leqslant 3(\delta^2 + P^2) + \frac{\delta^2 + Q^2}{3},\]
 so
 \begin{align*}
  \left(\sqrt{\delta^2 + P^2} + \sqrt{\delta^2 + Q^2}\right)^2 &= (\delta^2 + P^2) + (\delta^2 + Q^2) +  2\sqrt{(\delta^2 + P^2)(\delta^2 + Q^2)}\\
  &\leqslant 4(\delta^2 + P^2) + \frac{4}{3}(\delta^2 + Q^2)\\
  &= \frac{16}{3}\delta^2 + 4 P^2 + \frac{4}{3}Q^2.
 \end{align*}
On the other hand,
\[ \frac{4}{3}(4\delta^2 + (P+Q)^2) = \frac{16}{3}\delta^2 + \frac{4}{3}P^2 + \frac{8}{3}PQ + \frac{4}{3}Q^2,\]
and so
\[ \frac{4}{3}(4\delta^2 + (P+Q)^2) - (\sqrt{\delta^2 + P^2} + \sqrt{\delta^2 + Q^2})^2 \geqslant \frac{8}{3}P(Q - P) \geqslant 0.\]
Taking square roots proves the inequality.

label: lem:skewdeletionbound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:skewdeletionbound}
 Let $M = (m_{ij}) \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ be skew-symmetric, let $s \neq t$, and let $M'$ be obtained from $M$ by replacing the entries $m_{st}$ and $m_{ts}$ by $0$.  Then,
 \[ \left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \left\lVert M \right\rVert,\]
 and the constant $2/\sqrt{3}$ is sharp for every $n \geqslant 4$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin by proving that we can reduce to the $n = 4$ case with $s = 1$ and $t = 2$.  First, we may assume $n \geqslant 4$, since adjoining zero rows or columns changes neither $\left\lVert M \right\rVert$ nor $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert$.  Moreover, we can assume $M' \neq 0$.  Let $y,z \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be unit vectors with $y^tM'z = \left\lVert M' \right\rVert$.  If $e_s$ and $e_t$ denote standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^n$, then the subspace spanned by $e_s, e_t, y, z$ has dimension at most $4$, so it is contained in a $4$-dimensional subspace $W$ with an orthonormal basis $f_1 = e_s$, $f_2 = e_t$, $f_3$, $f_4$.  Let $U$ be the $n \times 4$ matrix with columns $f_1, f_2, f_3, f_4$, and define $N \colonequals U^tMU \in M_4(\mathbb{R})$.  Note that $N$ is skew-symmetric, since
 \[N^t = \left(U^tMU\right)^t = U^tM^tU = -U^tMU = -N.\]  Moreover, since $U$ has orthonormal columns,
 \[ \left\lVert N \right\rVert \leqslant \left\lVert U^t \right\rVert\left\lVert M \right\rVert\left\lVert U \right\rVert = \left\lVert M \right\rVert,\] and its $1,2$-entry is $e_s^tMe_t = m_{st}$.  Thus,
 \[ U^tM'U = U^tMU - m_{st}U^t(e_se_t^t - e_te_s^t)U = N',\]
 where $N'$ is obtained from $N$ by replacing the $1,2$- and $2,1$-entries by $0$.  There exist unit vectors $\hat{y}, \hat{z} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $y = U\hat{y}$, $z = U\hat{z}$, so
 \[ \left\lVert M' \right\rVert = y^t M' z = \hat{y}^tN'\hat{z} \leqslant \left\lVert N' \right\rVert.\]  Hence, it suffices to prove $\left\lVert N' \right\rVert \leqslant \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left\lVert N \right\rVert$ for skew-symmetric $N \in M_4(\mathbb{R})$ with $s = 1$ and $t = 2$.

 Let $N = (n_{ij})$.  Using the notation from Section \ref{sect:prelim}, we have
 \[F = F(N) = n_{12}^2 + n_{13}^2 + n_{14}^2 + n_{23}^2 + n_{24}^2 + n_{34}^2\]
 and
 \[ \operatorname{Pf} = \operatorname{Pf}(N) = n_{12}n_{34} - n_{13}n_{24} + n_{14}n_{23}.\]
 Defining
 \[ \eta \colonequals \frac{1}{2}(n_{12} + n_{34}, n_{13} - n_{24}, n_{14} + n_{23}), \quad \zeta \colonequals \frac{1}{2}(n_{12} - n_{34}, n_{13} + n_{24}, n_{14} - n_{23}) \in \mathbb{R}^3,\]
 we see that $|\eta|^2 + |\zeta|^2 = F/2$ and $|\eta|^2 - |\zeta|^2 = \operatorname{Pf}$, so
 \[ 4|\eta|^2|\zeta|^2 = \left(\frac{F}{2} \right)^2 - \operatorname{Pf}^2\]
 and
 \[ \left(|\eta| + |\zeta| \right)^2 = \frac{F}{2} + \sqrt{\frac{F^2}{4} - \operatorname{Pf}^2} = \frac{F + \sqrt{F^2 - 4\operatorname{Pf}^2}}{2} = s_1^2,\]
 the largest root of $x^2 - Fx + \operatorname{Pf}^2$ (see Proposition \ref{prop:skew}).  Hence,
 \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:normN}
  \left\lVert N \right\rVert = |\eta| + |\zeta|.
 \end{equation}
 Deleting $n_{12}$ replaces $\eta$ by $\eta' = \eta - (n_{12}/2,0,0)$ and $\zeta$ by $\zeta' = \zeta - (n_{12}/2, 0, 0)$; the first coordinates become, respectively, $n_{34}/2$ and $-n_{34}/2$, and the other coordinates do not involve $n_{12}$.  Define
 \[\delta \colonequals \frac{n_{34}}{2}, \quad P \colonequals \left\lVert \frac{1}{2}(n_{13} - n_{24}, n_{14} + n_{23}) \right\rVert, \quad Q \colonequals \left\lVert \frac{1}{2}(n_{13} + n_{24}, n_{14} - n_{23}) \right\rVert.\]
 Applying \eqref{eq:normN} to $N'$ and $N$, we have
 \begin{align*} \left\lVert N' \right\rVert &= \sqrt{\delta^2 + P^2} + \sqrt{\delta^2 + Q^2},\\
  \left\lVert N \right\rVert &= |(\frac{n_{12}}{2} + \delta, \frac{n_{13} - n_{24}}{2}, \frac{n_{14} + n_{23}}{2})| + |(\frac{n_{12}}{2} - \delta, \frac{n_{13} + n_{24}}{2}, \frac{n_{14} - n_{23}}{2})|\\
  &\geqslant |(2\delta, P + Q)| = \sqrt{4\delta^2 + (P+Q)^2};\\
 \end{align*}
 that
 \[\left\lVert N' \right\rVert \leqslant \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left\lVert N \right\rVert\]
 now follows from Lemma \ref{lem:ineq}.

 Finally, to get the sharpness of the inequality, take $n_{12} = 1/\sqrt{3}$, $n_{13} = 0$, $n_{14} = \sqrt{2/3}$, $n_{23} = -\sqrt{2/3}$, $n_{24} = 0$, and $n_{34} = -1/\sqrt{3}$.  Then, $\eta = (0,0,0)$ and $\zeta = (1/\sqrt{3}, 0, \sqrt{2/3})$, so $\left\lVert N \right\rVert = 1$ by \eqref{eq:normN}, while $\eta' = (-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}, 0, 0)$ and $\zeta' = (\frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}, 0, \sqrt{2/3})$, so \[\left\lVert N' \right\rVert = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}} + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\]
 We adjoin zero rows and columns when the matrix has dimension larger than $4$.

label: lem:normMandXi
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normMandXi}
 For every skew-symmetric $M \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $1 \leqslant k \leqslant r$,
 \[ \Xi_k(M) = \sum_{j = 0}^k (-1)^j {{r - j} \choose {k - j}} \varepsilon_j(M),\]
 and $\left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1$ if and only if $\Xi_k(M) \geqslant 0$ for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant r$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we note that the generating function for the elementary symmetric functions in variables $z_1, z_2, \dots, z_r$ is
 \[ P(t) = \sum_{k = 0}^r e_k(z_1, \dots, z_r) t^k = \prod_{j = 1}^r (1 + z_jt);\]
 see \cite[p. 20]{Mac15}.
 After substituting $z_j = 1 - x_j$, we have
 \[ P(t) = (1 + t)^r \prod_{j=1}^r \left(1 - \frac{t}{1 + t}x_j \right) = \sum_{j = 0}^r (-1)^j e_j(x_1, \dots, x_r)t^j(1+t)^{r-j}.\]
 Expanding $(1+t)^{r-j}$ using the Binomial Theorem, we get
 \[P(t) = \sum_{j = 0}^r (-1)^j e_j(x_1,\dots, x_r)t^j \sum_{m = 0}^{r-j} {{r-j} \choose m} t^m, \]
 and setting $j + m = k$, after comparing coefficients, we get
 \[ e_k(1- x_1, \dots, 1 - x_r) = \sum_{j = 0}^k (-1)^j {{r-j} \choose {k-j}} e_j(x_1, \dots, x_r).\]
 Setting $x_j = s_j^2$ for each $j$ so that $e_j(x_1, \dots, x_r) = \varepsilon_j(M)$, we see that
 \[ \Xi_k(M) = \sum_{j = 0}^k (-1)^j {{r - j} \choose {k - j}} \varepsilon_j(M).\]

 Assume $\left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1$, i.e., $s_j \leqslant 1$ for each $j$.  Since $1 - s_j^2 \geqslant 0$ for each $j$, $\Xi_k(M) = e_k(1 - s_1^2, \dots, 1 - s_r^2)$ is a sum of products of nonnegative numbers and hence is itself nonnegative.  Conversely, assume $\Xi_k(M) \geqslant 0$ for all $k$.  Define
 \[ p(t) = \prod_{j = 1}^r (t - (1 - s_j^2)) = \sum_{k=0}^r (-1)^k \Xi_k(M) t^{r - k},\]
 a monic polynomial with real roots, and assume $t < 0$.  Then, for each $k$, $(-1)^k \Xi_k(M) t^{r - k}$ has sign $(-1)^r$ or vanishes.  Since $p(t)$ is monic, $p$ is not identically $0$, and so $p(t)$ has sign $(-1)^r$, i.e., $p(t) \neq 0$ for all $t < 0$.  Hence, $p(t)$ has no negative roots, i.e., $1 - s_j^2 \geqslant 0$ for all $j$, and so $\left\lVert M \right\rVert = s_1 \leqslant 1$, as desired.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:matchings}
 Let $M$ be supported on a graph $G = (V,E)$ (that is, $m_{ij} = 0$ whenever $\{i,j\} \notin E$), and suppose that no subset of size $2k$ of $V$ induces a subgraph of $G$ with two distinct perfect matchings.  Then
 \[ \varepsilon_k(M) = \sum_{F} \prod_{f \in F} m_f^2,\]
 where the sum is over the sets $F$ of $k$ pairwise disjoint edges of $G$ and $m_f$ denotes the entry on the edge $f$.  In particular, the hypothesis holds when $G$ is a disjoint union of paths and when $G$ is an odd cycle.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n = 2r + 1$ and label the cycle $1 - 2 - \cdots - n - 1$, with $e = \{1, 2\}$.  Let $\left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1$, where $M = [A,D]$. Thus, $M' = [A,D']$ is $M$ with $m_{12}$ replaced by $0$, and it suffices to prove $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$.

 Both the odd cycle and the path remaining after the deletion of $e$ satisfy the hypothesis of Lemma \ref{lem:matchings}, and a set of $k$ disjoint edges of the cycle either avoids $e$ or consists of $e$ together with $k-1$ edges disjoint from $e$.  Let $S = \{3, 4, \dots, n\}$; note that $M_S$ is the matrix of the path $3 - 4 - \cdots - n$, whose edges are precisely those edges of the cycle that do not share a vertex with $e$.  Thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:matchings}, for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant r$,
 \[ \varepsilon_j(M) = \varepsilon_j(M') + m_{12}^2\varepsilon_{j-1}(M_S),\]
 i.e., $\varepsilon_j(M') = \varepsilon_j(M) - m_{12}^2 \varepsilon_{j-1}(M_S)$.  Thus, for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant r$,
 \begin{align*} \Xi_k(M') - \Xi_k(M) &= - \sum_{j = 1}^k (-1)^j {{r-j} \choose {k-j}} m_{12}^2 \varepsilon_{j-1}(M_S)\\
 &= m_{12}^2 \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1}(-1)^i {{(r-1) -i} \choose {(k-1) - i}}\varepsilon_i(M_S)\\
 &= m_{12}^2 \Xi_{k-1}(M_S) .
 \end{align*}
 By Lemma \ref{lem:compression}, $\left\lVert M_S \right\rVert \leqslant \left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1$, so  by Lemma \ref{lem:normMandXi} $\Xi_{k-1}(M_S) \geqslant 0$ for $1 \leqslant k-1 \leqslant r-1$, and $\Xi_0(M_S) = 1 > 0$.  Thus, $\Xi_k(M') \geqslant \Xi_k(M) \geqslant 0$ for every $k$, and $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:normMandXi}.

label: ex:C5
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:C5}
 For $n = 5$, we have $r = 2$, $\varepsilon_0(M) = 1$, \[\varepsilon_1(M) = m_{12}^2 + m_{23}^2 + m_{34}^2 + m_{45}^2 + m_{51}^2,\] \[\varepsilon_2(M) = m_{12}^2 m_{34}^2 + m_{23}^2 m_{45}^2 + m_{34}^2 m_{51}^2 + m_{45}^2 m_{12}^2 + m_{51}^2m_{23}^2,\]
 \[\Xi_1(M) = {2 \choose 1}\varepsilon_0(M) - {1 \choose 0}\varepsilon_1(M) = 2 - \varepsilon_1(M),\]
 \[ \Xi_2(M) = {2 \choose 2}\varepsilon_0(M) - {1 \choose 1}\varepsilon_1(M) + {0 \choose 0}\varepsilon_2(M) = 1 - \varepsilon_1(M) + \varepsilon_2(M).\]

 Set $S = \{3,4,5\}$.  Deleting $e = \{1, 2\}$ removes the term $m_{12}^2$ from $\varepsilon_1(M)$ and the terms $m_{12}^2 m_{34}^2$ and $m_{45}^2 m_{12}^2$ from $\varepsilon_2(M)$. Since
 \begin{align*} \Xi_1(M') &= 2 - \varepsilon_1(M')\\
                          &= 2 - \varepsilon_1(M) + m_{12}^2\\
                          &= \Xi_1(M) + m_{12}^2\Xi_0(M_S)\\
                          &\geqslant \Xi_1(M)\\
                          &\geqslant 0,
 \end{align*}
 and
 \begin{align*} \Xi_2(M') &= 1 - \varepsilon_1(M') + \varepsilon_2(M')\\
                          &= 1 - \varepsilon_1(M) + \varepsilon_2(M) + m_{12}^2 - m_{12}^2 m_{34}^2 - m_{45}^2 m_{12}^2\\
                          &= \Xi_2(M) + m_{12}^2\Xi_1(M_S)\\
                          &\geqslant \Xi_2(M)\\
                          &\geqslant 0,
 \end{align*}
by Lemma \ref{lem:normMandXi}, $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$, and any $A$ admissible for a Dirac operator $D$ of the $5$-cycle is admissible for the Dirac operator $D'$ obtained from $D$ by deleting $e$.

label: prop:signcrit
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:signcrit}
 Let $n = 2r$, let $D$ be a Dirac operator on the $n$-cycle, let $A$ be admissible for $D$, let $M = [A, D]$, and let $M'$ be obtained by deleting an edge.  If
 \[ (-1)^r m_{12}m_{23} \cdots m_{2r, 1} \geqslant 0,\]
 then $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$; that is, $A$ remains admissible after the edge deletion.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Relabeling the cycle if necessary, we may assume $e = \{1,2\}$; note that this does not change the product $m_{12}m_{23} \cdots m_{2r, 1}$.  As noted above, when $k < r$,
  $\Xi_k(M') \geqslant 0$, following the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:odd} mutatis mutandis.  When $k = r$, by \eqref{eq:Xir}, we have
  \[ \Xi_r(M') - \Xi_r(M) = m_{12}^2\Xi_{r-1}(M_S) + (-1)^r 2m_{12}m_{23} \cdots m_{2r,1},\]
  and both terms on the righthand side are nonnegative under the hypothesis.  By Lemma \ref{lem:normMandXi}, $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$.

label: eq:z1
title: Proof
body_md:
For $1 \leqslant i \leqslant n$, we set $z_i = a_i - a_{i+1}$; here, the indices are read modulo $n$, so $z_n = a_n - a_1$.  Thus, \[m_{i, i+1} = (a_i - a_{i+1})d_{i,i+1} = \frac{z_i}{w_{i,i+1}}.\]
 Moreover, since
 \[ \sum_{i = 1}^n z_i = 0\]
 and $d^{D}(1,2) = z_1 \geqslant 0$, we have
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eq:z1}
 d^{D}(1,2) = z_1 = \sum_{i = 2}^n w_{i,i+1}(-m_{i,i+1}) \leqslant \sum_{i = 2}^n w_{i,i+1} \mu_i.
  \end{equation}
Furthermore, $m_{12} \geqslant 0$ since $z_1, w_{12} \geqslant 0$.

 Assume first that $L(\mu) = 0$.  Since the nonzero entries of $L(\mu)$ are $\pm \mu_i$, this means $\mu = 0$, and so $m_{i,i+1} \geqslant 0$ for $i \geqslant 2$.  Hence $z_1 \leqslant 0$, i.e., $d^{D}(1,2) = z_1 = 0$.  Since $0 \leqslant 0 \cdot d^{D'}(1,2)$, the result holds trivially in this case.

 Otherwise, set $x = \mu/\left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert$, so $x_i \geqslant 0$ for each $i$ and $\left\lVert L(x) \right\rVert = 1$.  Deleting $e$ leaves the path $2 - 3 - \cdots - n - 1$, whose edges are $e_{23}, \dots, e_{n,1}$.  Define $B \colonequals \operatorname{diag}(b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n)$, where $b_2 = 0$ and $b_{i+1} = b_i - w_{i,i+1}x_i$ for $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n$ (again, subscripts are read modulo $n$).  Note that the entry of $[B,D']$ on $e_{i,i+1}$ for $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n$ is
 \[ (b_i - b_{i+1})d_i = w_{i,i+1}x_i/w_{i,i+1} = x_i.\]  Since $[B,D']$ has no other nonzero entries, $[B,D'] = L(x)$, i.e., $\left\lVert [B,D'] \right\rVert = \left\lVert L(x) \right\rVert = 1$, and $B$ is admissible for $D'$.  Telescoping along the path from vertex $2$ to vertex $1$, we have
 \[ d^{D'}(1,2) \geqslant |b_1 - b_2| = \left|\sum_{i=2}^{n} (b_i - b_{i+1})\right| = \sum_{i = 2}^n w_{i,i+1} x_i = \frac{1}{\left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert} \sum_{i = 2}^n w_{i,i+1} \mu_i \geqslant  \frac{d^{D}(1,2)}{\left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert},\]
 completing the proof.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n = 2r$ and label the cycle $1 - 2 - \cdots - n - 1$, and without loss of generality let $e = \{1, 2\}$.  We first treat the pair $\{x,y\} = \{1,2\}$.  Let $A$ be admissible for $D$ with $a_1 - a_2 = d^{D}(1,2)$; such an $A$ exists because the supremum in \eqref{eq:def} is attained (after normalizing $a_2 = 0$, the constraints $|a_i - a_{i+1}| \leqslant w_{i,i+1}$ confine the admissible diagonals to a compact set, on which $a_1 - a_2$ is continuous). Let $M = (m_{i,j}) = [A,D]$.  By Proposition \ref{prop:reduction}, we have $m_{12} \geqslant 0$.  Let $\mu_i = \max(-m_{i,i+1}, 0)$ for $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n$ (again, $m_{n, n+1} = m_{n,1}$) and set $\mu = (\mu_2, \dots, \mu_n)$.


 Suppose first that $m_{j,j+1} \geqslant 0$ for some $2 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.  Then, $\mu_j = 0$, and $L(\mu)$ is the direct sum of blocks corresponding to the maximal runs of consecutive nonzero entries of $\mu$, together with a zero block: the vertex sets of distinct runs are disjoint and no nonzero entry of $L(\mu)$ joins two of them, so the coordinate subspace spanned by the vertices of each run is invariant, and $\left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert$is the largest of the norms of the blocks.  It thus suffices to prove that $\left\lVert L(\nu) \right\rVert \leqslant 1$ for each run $\nu = (\mu_i, \mu_{i+1}, \dots, \mu_{i + k - 1}) \in \mathbb{R}^k$, all of whose entries are nonzero, where $k \leqslant n - 1$ and $L(\nu)$ denotes the skew-symmetric matrix of the path $i - (i + 1) - \cdots - (i + k)$ with entries $\nu$ and indices read modulo $n$.  In particular, since $\mu_j = 0$, it is impossible that both $i = 2$ and $i + k - 1 = n$.  Thus, if $T = \{i , i + 1, \dots, i + k\}$ is the set of the $k+1$ vertices of the run, then $T$ does not contain both $1$ and $2$.  Hence, the only edges of the cycle with both vertices in $T$ are $\{i, i+1\}, \dots, \{i + k -1, i + k\}.$  Since $\mu_\ell = -m_{\ell, \ell+1}$ for each $\ell$ in the run, $L(\nu) = -M_T$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:compression},
 \[ \left\lVert L(\nu) \right\rVert = \left\lVert M_T \right\rVert \leqslant \left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1.\]
 Hence, $\left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert \leqslant 1$ in this case, so by Proposition \ref{prop:reduction},
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant \left\lVert L(\mu) \right\rVert d^{D'}(1,2) \leqslant d^{D'}(1,2).\]

 Now suppose $m_{j,j+1} < 0$ for $2 \leqslant j \leqslant n$.  We already know that $m_{12} \geqslant 0$, and $r$ is odd, so
 \[ (-1)^rm_{12}m_{23} \cdots m_{n,1} \geqslant 0. \]
 By Proposition \ref{prop:signcrit}, $\left\lVert M' \right\rVert \leqslant 1$, meaning $A$ is admissible for $D'$ as well, and hence
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \leqslant d^{D'}(1,2)\]
 in any case.

 Finally, let $\{x,y\} \neq \{1,2\}$.  The graph obtained by deleting $e$ is the path $2 - 3 - \cdots - n - 1$, and the union of the simple paths from $x$ to $y$ is the path between $x$ and $y$, which contains $1$ and $2$ only when $\{x,y\} = \{1,2\}$.  The path is therefore an induced subgraph of the cycle, so, by Propositions \ref{prop:deletion} and \ref{prop:prune}, $d^{D'}(x,y) \geqslant d^{D}(x,y)$, completing the proof.

label: lem:weighting
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weighting}
 Let $M = (m_{ij})$ be a skew-symmetric matrix such that $m_{ij} = 0$ unless $j \equiv i \pm 1 \pmod n$, and let $w_{12}, \dots, w_{n,1}$ be a choice of weights for the $n$-cycle, where $w_{j,j+1}$ is the weight of $\{j, j+1\}$.  If $\left\lVert M \right\rVert \leqslant 1$ and $\sum_{i = 1}^n w_{i,i+1} m_{i,i+1} = 0$, then there exists an admissible diagonal matrix $A$ for $D$ such that $[A,D] = M$, and $d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant w_{12}m_{12}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We construct a specific admissible $A$ giving us $[A,D] = M$.  Define $a_1 \colonequals 0$ and $a_{i+1} \colonequals a_i - w_{i,i+1} m_{i,i+1}$ for $1 \leqslant i \leqslant n-1$, and let $A = \operatorname{diag}(a_1, \dots, a_n)$; indeed,
 \[ m_{i,i+1} = w_{i,i+1}m_{i,i+1}d_{i,i+1} = (a_i - a_{i+1})d_{i,i+1},\]
 and, since $\sum_{i = 1}^n w_{i,i+1} m_{i,i+1} = 0$,
 \[ m_{n,1} = d_{n,1}(w_{n,1} m_{n,1}) = d_{n,1}\left(-\sum_{i = 1}^{n-1}w_{i, i+1}m_{i, i+1}\right) = d_{n,1}a_{n} = (a_n - a_1)d_{n,1}.\]  All other entries of $[A,D]$ vanish, and $[A,D]$ is skew-symmetric; hence $[A,D] = M$, $A$ is admissible for $D$, and $d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant a_1 - a_2 = w_{12}m_{12}$.

label: lem:constantpath
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:constantpath}
 Let $c > 0$ and $\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ be the all-ones vector.  For $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$ the vector $g^{(k)} \in \mathbb{C}^n$ with entries $g_j^{(k)} = {\rm i}^{j-1}\sin(jk\theta)$ satisfies
 \[ L(c\mathbf{1})g^{(k)} = 2{\rm i} c \cos(k\theta) g^{(k)}.\]
 Consequently, the singular values of $L(c\mathbf{1})$ are the numbers $s_k \colonequals 2c\cos(k\theta)$, $1 \leqslant k \leqslant r$, each with multiplicity two, and they are positive and pairwise distinct.  Thus, $\left\lVert L(c\mathbf{1}) \right\rVert = 2c\cos \theta$, and, if $c^* = \frac{1}{2\cos(\theta)}$, $\left\lVert L(c^*\mathbf{1}) \right\rVert = 1$ and, in this case, for $2 \leqslant k \leqslant r$, the singular values are
 \[ s_k = \frac{\cos(k\theta)}{\cos \theta} < 1.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This is the idea used in the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.3]{CLPS25}.  If we define
 \[ Q \colonequals \operatorname{diag}({\rm i}, {\rm i}^2, \dots, {\rm i}^n),\]
 indexed along the path, then the matrix ${\rm i} Q^* L(c\mathbf{1}) Q$ is a real symmetric tridiagonal Toeplitz matrix, with all off-diagonal entries equal to $-c$.  We write $\omega_j = \sin(jk\theta)$, so that $\omega_0 = \omega_{n+1} = 0$ and $\omega_{j-1} + \omega_{j+1} = 2\cos(k\theta)\omega_j$.  With the convention $g_0^{(k)} = g_{n+1}^{(k)} = 0$, which is consistent with $\omega_0 = \omega_{n+1} = 0$, for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant n$, we have
 \begin{align*}
  \left(L(c\mathbf{1})g^{(k)}\right)_j &= cg_{j+1}^{(k)} - cg_{j-1}^{(k)} = c\left({\rm i}^j \omega_{j+1} - {\rm i}^{j-2}\omega_{j-1} \right)\\
   &= c {\rm i}^{j-1}{\rm i}\left(\omega_{j+1} + \omega_{j-1} \right) = 2{\rm i} c \cos(k\theta)g_j^{(k)},\\
 \end{align*}
using $-{\rm i}^{j-2} = {\rm i}^{j-1} \cdot {\rm i}$.  For $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, the values of $\cos(k \theta)$ are distinct since $0 < k\theta < \pi$, so this exhibits $n$ eigenvectors for $n$ distinct eigenvalues; hence, the spectrum of $L(c\mathbf{1})$ is $\{2 {\rm i} c \cos(k\theta): 1 \leqslant k \leqslant n\}$.  Since $\cos((n+1 - k)\theta) = -\cos(k\theta)$, the spectrum can be expressed as $\{\pm 2{\rm i} c \cos(k\theta): 1 \leqslant k \leqslant r\}$, and $\cos(k\theta) > 0$ for $k \leqslant r$ because $k\theta < \pi/2$ exactly when $2k < n+1$.  The result follows.
head: environment

label: lem:sine
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sine}
 For $1 \leqslant i \leqslant n$, define
 \[ \varpi_i \colonequals \sin((i-1)\theta)\sin(i\theta).\]
 If the path $2 - 3- \cdots - n - 1$ has a weight of $\varpi_j$ on the edge $\{j, j+1\}$ (where $\{n, n+1\} = \{n,1\}$), then
 \[ d^{D'}(1,2) = c^* \sum_{i = 1}^n \varpi_i.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed using the results of \cite[Section 3]{CLPS25} applied to the path with vertices $u_1 = 2, u_2 = 3, \dots, u_n = 1$; its $j^{\text{th}}$ edge is $\{j+1, j+2\}$ (read modulo $n$), and we write $d_j' = \varpi_{j+1}^{-1}$ for its Dirac entry, so that the vector $d$ as in \cite[Definition 3.4]{CLPS25} is $(d_1', \cdots, d_{n-1}')$.  Since
 \[ \frac{d_j'}{d_{j+1}'} = \frac{\varpi_{j+2}}{\varpi_{j+1}} = \frac{\sin((j+1)\theta)\sin((j+2)\theta)}{\sin(j\theta)\sin((j+1)\theta)} = \frac{h_{j+2}}{h_j},\]
 the products defining the vectors $\mu, \nu \in \mathbb{R}^r$ of \cite[Definition 3.4]{CLPS25} telescope:
 \[ \mu_{k+1} = \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{d_{2j-1}'}{d_{2j}'} = \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{h_{2j+1}}{h_{2j-1}} = \frac{h_{2k+1}}{h_1}, \quad \nu_{k+1} = \prod_{j=1}^k \frac{d_{2j}'}{d_{2j+1}'} = \frac{h_{2k+2}}{h_2}.\]
 Thus $\mu$ and $\nu$ are proportional to $h_{\text{odd}} = (h_1, h_3, \dots, h_{n-1})$ and $h_{\text{even}} = (h_2, h_4, \dots, h_n)$, and the unit vectors of \cite[Definition 3.18]{CLPS25} are $x = h_{\text{odd}}/\left\lVert h_{\text{odd}} \right\rVert$ and $y = h_{\text{even}}/\left\lVert h_{\text{even}} \right\rVert$.  Moreover, since $n+1$ is odd, the map $j \mapsto n + 1 - j$ exchanges odd and even indices, so $h_{n+1 - j} = \sin(\pi - j\theta) = h_j$, and hence $\left\lVert h_{\text{odd}} \right\rVert = \left\lVert h_{\text{even}} \right\rVert$.

 Let $z \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ have entries $z_j = c^*/d_j' = c^* \varpi_{j+1} > 0$, so that $z_jd_j' = c^*$ for every $j$.  The matrix $T(z)$ as defined in \cite[Definition 3.1]{CLPS25} is the $r \times r$ matrix
 \[ T(z) = \begin{bmatrix} d_1 z_1 & & \\ d_2 z_2 & d_3 z_3 & \\ & d_4 z_4 & d_5 z_5 & \\ & & & \ddots \end{bmatrix};\]
 here, it is the $r \times r$ matrix with $c^*$ on the diagonal and subdiagonal and $0$ elsewhere.  Since $h_0 = h_{n+1} = 0$, $h_{j-1} + h_{j+1} = 2h_j\cos\theta$, and $2c^*\cos \theta = 1$, for $1 \leqslant k \leqslant r$, we have
 \[ \left( T(z) h_{\text{even}}\right)_k = c^*(h_{2k - 2} + h_{2k}) = h_{2k-1}, \quad \left( T(z)^t h_{\text{odd}}\right)_k = c^*(h_{2k -1} + h_{2k + 1}) = h_{2k}.\]
 Since $\left\lVert h_{\text{odd}} \right\rVert = \left\lVert h_{\text{even}} \right\rVert$, this says $T(z)y = x$ and $T(z)^tx = y$.  As $z$ has no zero entries, it is viable in the sense of \cite[Definition 3.8]{CLPS25}, so, by \cite[Proposition 3.19]{CLPS25}, $d^{D'}(u_1, u_n) = \left\lVert \mu \right\rVert\left\lVert \nu \right\rVert/d_1'$.  Finally, by \cite[Lemma 3.5]{CLPS25},
 \[ d_1' \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} z_j = \mu^t T(z) \nu = \left\lVert \mu \right\rVert\left\lVert \nu \right\rVert x^t T(z) y = \left\lVert \mu \right\rVert\left\lVert \nu \right\rVert x^t x = \left\lVert \mu \right\rVert\left\lVert \nu \right\rVert,\]
 so \[d^{D'}(1,2) = d^{D'}(u_1, u_n) = \sum_{j = 1}^{n-1} z_j = c^* \sum_{i = 2}^n \varpi_i,\]
 and the result follows since $\varpi_1 = 0$.

label: rem:simplification
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:simplification}
 In fact, $d^{D'}(1,2) = (n+1)/4$ in Lemma \ref{lem:sine}.  Indeed, since
 \[ \sin((i-1)\theta)\sin(i\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\cos \theta - \cos((2i-1)\theta) \right)\]
 and
 \[ 2\sin\theta \sum_{i = 1}^n \cos((2i-1)\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(\sin(2i\theta) - \sin((2i -2)\theta) \right) = \sin(2n\theta) = -\sin(2\theta),\]
 we have
 \[ \sum_{i=1}^n \cos((2i - 1)\theta) = - \cos\theta, \]
 and hence
 \[ \sum_{i=1}^n \varpi_i = \frac{n\cos\theta}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n \cos((2i-1)\theta) = \frac{n\cos \theta}{2} + \frac{\cos \theta}{2} = \frac{(n+1)\cos\theta}{2},\]
 and, therefore,
 \[ d^{D'}(1,2) = c^* \sum_{i = 1}^n \varpi_i = \frac{n+1}{4}.\]

label: prop:witness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:witness}
 Let $\delta > 0$ and define $\gamma \colonequals c^*(1 + \delta)$.  If $\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1}$, $\chi(\delta) \colonequals -\Xi_r\left(L(\gamma \mathbf{1}) \right)$, $t(\delta) \colonequals \chi(\delta)/\gamma^{n-1}$, and the skew-symmetric matrix $M = (m_{ij}) \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is defined by $m_{12} = t(\delta)$, $m_{23} = m_{34} = \cdots = m_{n,1} = -\gamma$, and $m_{i,j} = 0$ otherwise, then for sufficiently small $\delta > 0$, $t(\delta) > 0$ and $\left\lVert M \right\rVert < 1$.
head: environment

label: eq:Xir2
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M$ be as in the statement, $M' = L(-\gamma \mathbf{1})$ be the matrix obtained from $M$ by deleting the edge $\{1,2\}$, and let $M_S$ be the compression of $M$ to the set $S = \{3, \dots, n\}$; note that neither $M'$ nor $M_S$ depend on $t(\delta)$.  Since
 \[ m_{12}m{23} \cdots m_{n,1} = t(\delta) \cdot (-\gamma)^{n-1} = -t(\delta) \cdot \gamma^{n-1},\]
 the identity \eqref{eq:Xir} yields
 \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:Xir2}
  \Xi_r(M) = \Xi_r(M') - t(\delta)^2\Xi_{r-1}(M_S) + (-1)^r 2t(\delta)\gamma^{n-1}.
 \end{equation}
 By Lemma \ref{lem:constantpath}, the $k^\text{th}$ singular value of $M'$ is $s_k(M') = (1 + \delta)\cos(k\theta)/\cos(\theta)$, so, by the definition of $\Xi_r$, we have
 \[ \chi(\delta) = -\Xi_r(M') = -(1 - (1 + \delta)^2) \prod_{k=2}^r \left( 1 - (1 + \delta)^2\frac{\cos^2(k\theta)}{\cos^2 \theta}\right).\]
 The first factor is $-(1 - (1 + \delta)^2) = 2\delta + \delta^2$ and the others tend to $1 - \cos^2(k\theta)/\cos^2(\theta) > 0$ as $\delta \to 0$.  Hence, for small $\delta$, $\chi(\delta) > 0$ and so $t(\delta) > 0$; moreover, $\chi(\delta) \to 0$ and $t(\delta) \to 0$. Furthermore, \eqref{eq:Xir2} becomes
 \[ \Xi_r(M) = -\chi(\delta) + 2\chi(\delta) - t(\delta)^2 \Xi_{r-1}(M_S) = \chi(\delta) \left(1 - \frac{\chi(\delta)\Xi_{r-1}(M_S)}{\gamma^{2(n-1)}} \right),\]
 and $(1 - \chi(\delta)\Xi_{r-1}(M_S)/\gamma^{2(n-1)} \to 1$ as $\delta \to 0$, so $\Xi_r(M) > 0$ for small $\delta$.

 Finally, if $X$ is skew-symmetric, then ${\rm i} X$ is Hermitian, and applying Weyl's inequality \cite[Theorem 4.3.1]{HJ13} to ${\rm i} X$, whose second largest eigenvalue is the second largest singular value $s_2(X)$ of $X$, we see that the map $s_2$ sending $X$ to its second largest singular value is $1$-Lipschitz for the operator norm.  Since $M - L(-c*\mathbf{1}) = t(\delta)\left(E_{1,2} - E_{2,1}\right) + L(-c^*\delta\mathbf{1})$ has norm at most $t(\delta) + 2c^*\delta \cos \theta = t(\delta) + \delta$, Lemma \ref{lem:constantpath} gives
 \[ s_2(M) \leqslant \frac{\cos(2\theta)}{\cos \theta} + t(\delta) + \delta < 1\]
 for small $\delta$.  Then, for $j \geqslant 2$ the factors $1 - s_j(M)^2$ of $\Xi_r(M) = \prod_{j = 1}^r \left(1 - s_j(M)^2\right)$ are positive, and so $\Xi_r(M) > 0$ forces $1 - s_1^2(M) > 0$, i.e., $\left\lVert M \right\rVert < 1$.

label: thm:0mod4
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\delta > 0$ and define $\gamma$ and $t(\delta)$ as in the statement of Proposition \ref{prop:witness}.  Define weights $w_{j,j+1}$ for the edge $\{j, j+1\}$ of the $n$-cycle by $w_{i,i+1} = \varpi_i = \sin((i-1)\theta)\sin(i\theta)$ for $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n$ and
 \[w_{12} = \frac{c^*(1+\delta)}{t(\delta)}\sum_{i = 2}^n \varpi_i = \frac{(1 + \delta)(n+1)}{4t(\delta)},\]
 where the last equality follows from Remark \ref{rem:simplification}.  Define $M = (m_{i,j})$ as in the statement of Proposition \ref{prop:witness}.  Then, for sufficiently small $\delta > 0$, $\left\lVert M \right\rVert < 1$, and, by the choice of $w_{12}$,
 \[ \sum_{i = 1}^n w_{i,i+1} m_{i,i+1} = w_{12} t(\delta) - \gamma \sum_{i = 2}^n \varpi_i = \frac{(1 + \delta)(n+1)}{4} - \frac{(1 + \delta)(n+1)}{4} = 0.\]  Thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:weighting}, there exists an admissible diagonal matrix $A$ such that $[A,D] = M$, and, moreover,
 \[ d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant w_{12} m_{12} = \frac{(1 + \delta)(n+1)}{4} > \frac{n+1}{4} = d^{D'}(1,2),\]
 where the last equality follows from Remark \ref{rem:simplification}.  The result follows.

label: prop:safe
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:safe}
 Let $e \in E$, $x, y \in V$, $D$ be a Dirac operator for $G$, and $D'$ the Dirac operator for $G - e$ obtained after deleting $e$.  Suppose that, after pruning, the path space $\mathbb{P}_{G - e}(x,y)$ is an induced subgraph of $G$.  Then, $d^{D'}(x,y) \geqslant d^{D}(x,y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By Proposition \ref{prop:prune}, $d^{D'}(x,y) = d^{D''}(x,y)$, where $D''$ is induced on $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(x,y)$.  By Proposition \ref{prop:deletion}, the distance on an induced subgraph of $G$ is at least $d^{D}(x,y)$.
head: environment

label: cor:necessary
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:necessary}
 Let $e \in E(G)$, $x, y \in V(G)$, $D$ be a Dirac operator for $G$, and $D'$ the Dirac operator for $G - e$ obtained after deleting $e$.  If $d^{D'}(x,y) < d^{D}(x,y)$, then both endpoints of $e$ lie in $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(x,y)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $S$ be the vertex set of $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(x,y)$, so that $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(x,y) = (G - e)[S]$.  Since $D$ and $D'$ differ only in the two entries corresponding to $e$, if $e$ does not have both endpoints in $S$, then the compressions $D_S'$ and $D_S$ coincide. Equivalently, $(G - e)[S] = G[S]$, so $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(x,y)$ is an induced subgraph of $G$.  The result follows from Proposition \ref{prop:safe}.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: If $G$ is the $4$-cycle $1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 1$, the deletion of $e = \{1,2\}$ leaves $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(1,3)$ equal to the path $1 - 4 - 3$, which does not contain the vertex $2$; similarly, $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(1,4)$ does not contain $2$, $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(2,3)$ and $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(2,4)$ do not contain $1$, and $\mathbb{P}_{G-e}(3,4)$ contains neither $1$ nor $2$.  Hence, by Corollary \ref{cor:necessary}, the distance can only possibly decrease between the vertices $1$ and $2$, i.e., in a $4$-cycle, the distance between two vertices can only possibly decrease between the two endpoints of the deleted edge.

label: prop:pendant
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:pendant}
 Let $G$ be a weighted graph, $e \in E(G)$, $x, y \in V(G)$, $D$ the Dirac operator of $G$, $D'$ the Dirac operator of $G - e$, and suppose
 \[ d^{D}(x,y) - d^{D'}(x,y) > 0.\]
 Let $G^+$ be obtained from $G$ by attaching a path $P_x$ at $x$, ending at a new vertex $x'$, and a path $P_y$ at $y$, ending at a new vertex $y'$, where all vertices of $P_x$ and $P_y$ other than $x$ and $y$ are new and distinct; let $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$ denote the total weights of $P_x$ and $P_y$, let $D^+$ be the Dirac operator of $G^+$, and let $D''$ be the Dirac operator of $G^+ - e$.  If $\delta_x + \delta_y < d^{D}(x,y) - d^{D'}(x,y)$, then
 \[ d^{D+}(x', y') \geqslant d^{D}(x,y) > d^{D'}(x,y) + \delta_x + \delta_y \geqslant d^{D''}(x',y').\]
 In particular, \eqref{eq:question} also fails for $G^+$, $e$, and the pair $(x', y')$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The second inequality follows immediately from the hypotheses.  We consider next the first inequality.  Let $A = \operatorname{diag}(a)$ be admissible for $G$ with $a_x - a_y = d^{D}(x,y)$, and extend $a$ to $a^+$ by assigning the value $a_x$ to every vertex of $P_x$ and the value $a_y$ to every vertex of $P_y$, and set $A^+ = \operatorname{diag}(a^+)$.  Every new commutator entry is of the form $(a_u - a_v)d_{uv}$ with $a_u = a_v$ and hence vanishes, so $[A^+, D^+]$ is $[A,D]$ bordered by zero rows and columns, and furthermore $\left\lVert [A^+, D^+] \right\rVert = \left\lVert [A,D] \right\rVert \leqslant 1$.  Since $a_{x'} - a_{y'} = a_x - a_y$, the claim follows from \eqref{eq:def}.

 For the third inequality, we note that no simple path of $G^+ - e$ from $x$ to $y$ enters $P_x$ or $P_y$, so $\mathbb{P}_{G^+ - e}(x,y) = \mathbb{P}_{G - e}(x,y)$ and, by Proposition \ref{prop:prune}, $d^{D''}(x,y) = d^{D'}(x,y)$.  Furthermore, by Proposition \ref{prop:geod}, $d^{D''}(x,x') \leqslant \ell^{D''}(x,x') \leqslant \delta_x$ and $d^{D''}(y,y') \leqslant \ell^{D''}(y,y') \leqslant \delta_y$.  The triangle inequality for $d^{D''}$ now yields $d^{D''}(x',y') \leqslant \delta_x + d^{D'}(x,y) + \delta_y$, completing the proof.

label: cor:nonincident
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $G^+$ have vertices $x, 1, 2, 3, 4, y$ and weights $w_{x,1} = w_{2,y} = 1/10$, $w_{12} = 5$, and $w_{23} = w_{34} = w_{41} = 1$, and let $e = \{1,2\}$.  Consider first the induced subgraph $G$ on $\{1,2,3,4\}$; it is a $4$-cycle, and we will denote the Dirac operator of $G$ by $D$.  By Theorem \ref{thm:main} with $\varepsilon = 1/5$, we have $d^{D}(1,2) \geqslant \sqrt{5}$ and $d^{D'}(1,2) = 2$, where $D'$ is the Dirac operator of $G - e$.  Noting that $\sqrt{5} - 2 > 1/5$ and that $P_x$, $P_y$ each consist of a single edge, we can apply Proposition \ref{prop:pendant} by giving the weight $\delta_x = \delta_y = 1/10$ to each of $\{x,1\}$ and $\{2,y\}$.  The result follows.

label: lem:blowup
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: blow up

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Gamma = \prod_{i = 0}^r {\rm Sym}(L_i) \leqslant {\rm Aut}(G)$; note that $\Gamma$ fixes $x$ and $y$, since $L_p$ and $L_{p'}$ are singletons.  The set
 \[ \mathcal{K} = \{ a \in \mathbb{R}^{V(G)}: \left\lVert [\operatorname{diag}(a),D] \right\rVert \leqslant 1\}\] is convex and invariant under the action of $\Gamma$, and the objective $a_x - a_y$ is $\Gamma$-invariant.  Since $H$ is connected, so is $G$, and the supremum in \eqref{eq:def} is attained (see, for instance, \cite[Section 2.3]{CLPS25}); hence, averaging a maximizing $a$ over $\Gamma$ produces a maximizing $\overline{a} \in \mathcal{K}$ that is constant on each $L_i$.

 Let $a$ be constant on each $L_i$ with value $\alpha_i$ and let $M = (m_{uv}) = [A,D]$, so $m_{uv} = (\alpha_i - \alpha_j)C_{ij}$ for $u \in L_i$ and $v \in L_j$.  If $e_u$ is the standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^{V(G)}$ at the vertex $u$, we define
 \[ b_i \colonequals k_i^{-1/2} \sum_{u \in L_i} e_u,\]
 so $b_i$ is the normalized indicator vector of $L_i$, and define $U \colonequals {\rm span}\{b_0, \dots, b_r\}$.  Thus, $U$ consists of the vectors that are constant on each $L_i$, and $U^\perp$ consists of the vectors whose entries sum to zero over each $L_i$; that is, $U^\perp$ is spanned by the vectors $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^{V(G)}$ that are supported on a single layer $L_i$ and satisfy $\sum_{u \in L_i} \xi_u = 0$.

 Let $\xi$ be such a vector, supported on $L_i$.  For $v \in L_j$,
 \[ (M\xi)_v = \sum_{u \in L_i} m_{vu}\xi_u = (\alpha_j - \alpha_i)C_{ij} \sum_{u \in L_i} \xi_u = 0,\] and, for $v \in L_i$, $(M\xi)_v = 0$ as well, since there are no edges inside $L_i$.  Hence, $M|_{U^\perp} = 0$.  Moreover, for $v \in L_j$,
 \[ (Mb_i)_v = k_i^{-1/2} \sum_{u \in L_i} m_{vu} = k_i^{-1/2} \cdot k_i(\alpha_j -\alpha_i)C_{ij} = k_i^{1/2}(\alpha_j - \alpha_i)C_{ij},\]
 which is constant on $L_j$, so
 \[ Mb_i = \sum_{j = 0}^r \sqrt{k_i k_j} (\alpha_j - \alpha_i) C_{ij}b_j.\]
 Thus, $U$ is $M$-invariant, and, since $\mathbb{R}^{V(G)} = U \oplus U^\perp$ and $M|_{U^\perp} = 0$, $\left\lVert M \right\rVert = \left\lVert M|_U \right\rVert$.  In the orthonormal basis $b_0, \dots, b_r$, the $j,i$-entry of $M|_U$ is $\sqrt{k_i k_j} (\alpha_j - \alpha_i) C_{ij}$, so $M|_U$ is exactly the commutator of $\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_0, \dots, \alpha_r)$ with the Dirac operator $\tilde{C}$ of $\tilde{H}$, whose entries are $\sqrt{k_ik_j} C_{ij}$.  Finally, $a_x - a_y = \alpha_p - \alpha_{p'}$ because $L_p = \{x\}$ and $L_{p'} = \{y\}$, and every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^{r+1}$ arises from an $a$ that is constant on each $L_i$.  Therefore, $d^{D}(x,y) = d^{\tilde{C}}(h_p, h_{p'}).$

label: thm:nonlocal
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, (i) follows from the fact that all edges in $G$ have weight $1$, and every path from either $x$ or $y$ to $z$ uses exactly $q+1$ of the edges.

 For (ii), by Lemma \ref{lem:blowup} with layer sizes of $k$ for all $A_i, B_i$ and $1$ for $x, y, z$, we have $d^{D}(x,y) = d^{\tilde{C}}(x,y)$, where $\tilde{C}$ is the Dirac operator of the cycle
 \[ x \overset{1/\sqrt{k}}{-} A_1 \overset{1/k}{-} \cdots \overset{1/k}{-} A_q \overset{1/\sqrt{k}}{-} z \overset{1/\sqrt{k}}{-} B_q \overset{1/k}{-} \cdots \overset{1/k}{-} B_1 \overset{1/\sqrt{k}}{-} y \overset{1}{-} x,\]
 since edges adjoining a singleton to a set of size $k$ acquire the factor $\sqrt{k}$, and edges adjoining two sets of size $k$ acquire the factor $k$.  By Proposition \ref{prop:geod}, \[d^{\tilde{C}}(x,y) \leqslant \ell^{\tilde{C}}(x,y) \leqslant \frac{4}{\sqrt{k}} + \frac{2(q-1)}{k}.\]

 Finally, (iii) follows from Proposition \ref{prop:prune}, noting that $\mathbb{P}_{G-z}(x,y) = \{x,y\}$ and $w_{xy} = 1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
A weak form of locality does in fact hold once the maximal degree of the graph is controlled: a distant vertex can change a noncommutative distance only by a bounded factor.  Indeed, if $z$ is far enough from $x$ and $y$ that $\ell_{V'}^{D}(x,y) = \ell^D(x,y)$, then combining Proposition \ref{prop:geod} with \cite[Theorem 5]{Bes21} gives
 \[ \frac{d_{V'}^D(x,y)}{d^{D}(x,y)} \leqslant \frac{\ell_{V'}{D}(x,y)}{\ell^D(x,y)/\Delta(G)} = \Delta(G),\]
 where $\Delta(G)$ denotes the maximum degree of $G$.

 In Theorem \ref{thm:nonlocal}, we have $\Delta(G_{q,k}) = 2k$, and the ratio is on the order of $\sqrt{\Delta(G)}$ for $q$ fixed.  Indeed, assume $k \geqslant (2q + 2)^2$ so that $4/\sqrt{k} + 2(q-1)/k \leqslant 1$.  By Lemma \ref{lem:blowup}, $d^{D}(x,y) = d^{\tilde{C}}(x,y)$, where $\tilde{C}$ is the weighted cycle in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:nonlocal}.  Since $\Delta(\tilde{C}) = 2$ and \[\ell^{\tilde{C}}(x,y) = \min(1, 4/\sqrt{k} + 2(q-1)/k) = 4/\sqrt{k} + 2(q-1)/k,\]
 by \cite[Theorem 5]{Bes21} and Proposition \ref{prop:geod}, we have
 \[ 2/\sqrt{k} + (q-1)/k \leqslant d^{D}(x,y) \leqslant 4/\sqrt{k} + 2(q-1)/k.\]  Finally, since
 \[ \frac{4}{\sqrt{k}} \leqslant 4/\sqrt{k} + 2(q-1)/k \leqslant \frac{2q + 2}{\sqrt{k}},\]
 it follows that
 \[ \frac{\sqrt{\Delta(G)}}{(2q + 2)\sqrt{2}} \leqslant \frac{d_{V'}^D(x,y)}{d^{D}(x,y)} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\Delta(G)}}{2\sqrt{2}}, \]
i.e., the ratio is on the order of $\sqrt{\Delta(G)}$ (as opposed to $\Delta(G)$).  It would be interesting to know whether the bound of $\Delta(G)$ can actually be attained or whether the correct bound happens to be $\sqrt{\Delta(G)}$, and it would be interesting to know whether the ratio tends to one as the distance from $z$ to $x$ and $y$ goes to infinity when $\Delta(G)$ is bounded.

label: thm:farweight
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The vertex set is partitioned into $\{x\}$, $L_1$, $\{1\}$, $\{2\}$, $\{3\}$, $\{4\}$, $L_2$, $\{y\}$, no set contains an edge, and sets adjacent in $H$ are completely joined with edges of constant weight; thus, Lemma \ref{lem:blowup} applies with $k_{L_1} = k_{L_2} = k$ and all other $k_i = 1$.  Since $x$ and $y$ lie in singleton sets, $d^{D}(x,y) = d^{C}(x,y)$, where $C$ is the Dirac operator of $H$, which is the quotient
 \[
  x\overset{W/\sqrt k}{-\!\!-}L_1\overset{W/\sqrt k}{-\!\!-}1
  \ \bigl[\,\text{$4$-cycle }5,1,1,1\,\bigr]\
  2\overset{W/\sqrt k}{-\!\!-}L_2\overset{W/\sqrt k}{-\!\!-}y .
\]
The edge $e$ joins two singleton sets, so $G - e$ is the blow-up of $H - e$ with the same set sizes, and, likewise, $d^{D'}(x,y) = d^{C'}(x,y)$, where $D'$ and $C'$ denote the Dirac operators of $G - e$ and $H - e$, respectively.

It hence suffices to prove the two inequalities in $H$.  Let $G_0$ be the $4$-cycle on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ with the stated weights; let $D_0$ be its Dirac operator, and let $D_0'$ be the Dirac operator of $G_0 - e$.  By Theorem \ref{thm:main} with $\varepsilon = 1/5$ we have $d^{D_0}(1,2) \geqslant \sqrt{5}$ and $d^{D_0'}(1,2) = 2$, so $d^{D_0}(1,2) - d^{D_0'}(1,2) > 1/5$.  The graph $H$ is obtained from $G_0$ by attaching at $1$ the path $1 - L_1 - x$ and at $2$ the path $2 - L_2 - y$, of total weights $\delta_x = \delta_y = 2W/\sqrt{k} \leqslant 1/10$ (since $k \geqslant 400W^2$); hence, \[\delta_x + \delta_y \leqslant \frac{1}{5} < d^{D_0}(1,2) - d^{D_0'}(1,2),\]
and, by Proposition \ref{prop:pendant}, we have
\[ d^{C'}(x,y) \leqslant d^{D_0'}(1,2) + \delta_x + \delta_y \leqslant \frac{11}{5} < \sqrt{5} \leqslant d^{D_0}(1,2) \leqslant d^{C}(x,y).\]
Finally, the only neighbors of $x$ are the vertices of $L_1$, each of whose only other neighbor is $1$, so $\ell^D(x,1) = 2W$, and, similarly, $\ell^D(y,2) = 2W$.

body_md:
\label{rem:combined}
 Both the graph-theoretic and the weighted distance can be made large simultaneously: replacing each of $L_1$ and $L_2$ by a chain of $q$ sets, each of size $k$, as in Theorem \ref{thm:nonlocal} gives attaching paths of total weight $2W/\sqrt{k} + (q-1)W/k$ in the quotient while $e$ sits at graph-theoretic distance $q+1$ and weighted distance $(q+1)W$ from each of $x$ and $y$.  Again, this construction requires both $x$ and $y$ to have large degree.
